hints: Notice the question asks for the one expression that does not equal the rate of transfer of energy in $\text{J s}^{-1}$ or $\text{W}$.
Recall that $work\ done = force \times displacement$ and that dividing an energy transfer by $time$ gives power.
Check each option by substitution or by units: see what $(force \times displacement)/time$ simplifies to, and what units $work\ done \times velocity$ would have.
walkthrough: Start from the definition: power is the rate of doing work, $P = work\ done / time$, with unit watt ($\text{W}$) equal to $\text{J s}^{-1}$.
Since $work\ done = force \times displacement$ in the direction of the force, then $P = (force \times displacement)/time$ is also correct.
For motion at steady velocity $v$, $displacement/time = v$, so $P = force \times (displacement/time) = force \times velocity$.
Test the remaining expression by units: $work\ done \times velocity$ has units $\text{J} \times \text{m s}^{-1} = \text{kg m}^{3} \text{s}^{-3}$, not $\text{kg m}^{2} \text{s}^{-3}$ for the watt.
Therefore only $work\ done \times velocity$ cannot be used to calculate power. This is option D.

options.A: This gives power because $force \times displacement$ is work done, and work done divided by $time$ is power.
options.B: This gives power for a force moving at velocity $v$, since $P = W/t = Fs/t = Fv$ when force and velocity are parallel.
options.C: This is the definition of power as the rate of doing work, with unit $\text{W}$ or $\text{J s}^{-1}$.
options.D: This cannot give power because $work \times velocity$ has units $\text{J} \times \text{m s}^{-1}$, which is not the watt.
